idiom_name: ASP.NET Core policy-based authorization (authorization middleware + IAuthorizationHandler)
implementation_notes: ASP.NET Core's authorization middleware is the enforcement point: endpoint metadata selects a named, default or fallback policy, and each IAuthorizationRequirement is evaluated by one or more IAuthorizationHandler instances. Apply policies with [Authorize(Policy = "...")] or RequireAuthorization("...") and register them with AddAuthorizationBuilder().AddPolicy(...); an authenticated failure becomes 403 while an unauthenticated request is challenged as 401. Set a fallback policy so endpoints with no authorization metadata are not accidentally public, and keep requirements/handlers responsible for decisions rather than controller bodies.
pitfalls: Registering a requirement without its handler -> no code succeeds the requirement and the policy denies everyone -> register the handler with DI and test an allow case.
Forgetting endpoint metadata and leaving fallback policy unset -> a new endpoint is reachable without authorization -> set a secure fallback policy and opt out only with [AllowAnonymous].

Swallowing a backend lookup exception or succeeding by default -> a data failure can silently become the wrong decision -> fail closed and surface the operational error without leaking it to the caller.

variants.name: Declarative policy pipeline ([Authorize]/RequireAuthorization + handlers)
Imperative resource-based authorization (IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync)
variants.implementation_notes: Attribute evaluation runs before model binding and before any resource is loaded, so a decision that depends on the resource itself cannot be expressed with [Authorize]: inject IAuthorizationService and call AuthorizeAsync(user, resource, "SameAuthorPolicy"), then branch on AuthorizationResult.Succeeded and return 403 yourself where the framework would otherwise have done it. The policy and its handler classes are the same decision machinery as the declarative variant - only the enforcement call moves into the operation, which is how ASP.NET Core covers object-level access. Prefer the declarative variant whenever the request alone carries enough context; use this one when it does not.
pitfalls: An imperative check placed after a state change leaves a write committed before the decision -> read first, decide, then write.
Forbid() only produces 403 when the authentication scheme is known; in minimal APIs route through the framework's result helpers instead of writing a bare status code.
Scattering AuthorizeAsync calls per operation reassembles the scattering the pattern removes: keep the policy names and requirements central and call them from one service-level guard where possible.
